raw.title: Large Language Models as Falsifiers for Cyber-Physical Systems
raw.body: Falsification searches for counterexamples to formal specifications in cyber-physical systems (CPS). With specifications written in Signal Temporal Logic (STL), falsification can be formulated as a robustness optimization problem, traditionally tackled with black-box search algorithms. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as surprisingly effective optimizers when coupled with iterative prompting. In this work, we connect these ideas and introduce LLM-Falsifier, an LLM-based approach that falsifies specifications by minimizing the STL robustness degree. Beyond generic prompt-based optimization, our key idea is to expose the LLM to semantic information that is natural for language models but absent from standard numerical optimizers, including natural-language input and output names, output trajectories, and critical-time witnesses for the minimum robustness value. These additions enable smarter and more sample-efficient robustness search. On the ARCH-COMP falsification benchmarks, LLM-Falsifier is shown to outperform existing falsification tools based on a range of optimization paradigms, from surrogate-based and Bayesian optimization to search-based testing, on 14 of 21 specifications when measured by the average number of simulations required to find a counterexample.

analysis.one_line_summary: LLM으로 CPS 검증, 시뮬 비용 절감

key_points.point: LLM-Falsifier는 LLM을 이용해 STL 강건성 지수를 최소화함으로써 CPS 규격을 위반하는 사례를 찾는다.
자연어 입력·출력 이름, 궤적, 최소 강건성 시점 등 의미 정보를 LLM에 제공해 샘플 효율성을 높인다.
ARCH‑COMP 벤치마크에서 21개 규격 중 14개에서 기존 도구보다 평균 시뮬레이션 수가 적게 소요되었다.

analysis.positioning: CPS의 형식적 규격 검증은 STL 기반 강건성 최적화로 접근해 왔으며, 기존에는 블랙박스 탐색·베이지안 등 수치 최적화에 의존했다. 본 논문은 LLM을 프롬프트 기반 최적화기로 활용해 의미 정보를 결합, 샘플 효율성을 크게 개선한 연구이며, LLM 활용 검증 흐름의 새로운 단계로 자리한다.
production_ideas: LLM 기반 의미 정보를 활용해 자율주행 경로 계획 시뮬레이션 횟수를 줄이는 최적화 도구를 만든다.
데이터 파이프라인의 컬럼명·샘플 데이터를 LLM에 제공해 하이퍼파라미터 탐색을 효율화한다.
API 계약 위반 메트릭을 최소화하도록 LLM에게 엔드포인트명·예시 페이로드를 입력해 테스트 케이스 자동 생성한다.

[43:07] And with that, as a final piece, let's step back and summarize everything we just did, because it's actually a lot.
[43:13] The problem itself asked for the smallest number of tiles that leaves one gap per column and one gap per row. Our claim is that that smallest number of tiles comes from this special grid pattern. The very pleasing one, filled with square tiles of side length K, where we counted the total number of tiles used is K squared plus 2K minus 3.
[43:33] To prove it, we spent most of the first half of this video leading up to and motivating this diagram here. And that's where the actual proof that you would write down begins. You would say, for any possible tiling, consider the gaps that they leave, these grid squares that we're marking with X's, and draw two distinct paths. One that connects a longest increasing subsequence, and one that connects a longest decreasing subsequence.
[43:57] Those two paths divide the diagram into four separate regions, which we then used to define a special subset of all of the edges of the X-ed out squares that we want to highlight. Highlight the right edges when they're in the right region, top edges when they're in the top region, perhaps two edges when they're on the boundaries. You remember all those rules.
[44:15] The reason we did all that was that we could argue that each such highlighted edge corresponds to a unique tile, meaning the number of tiles is at least as big as the number of highlighted edges. From there, we worked out the number of highlighted edges to be K squared plus the length of that longest increasing subsequence, plus the length of the longest decreasing subsequence, all minus four. Moreover, if those paths intersect, you actually get to add one on and this becomes a minus three.
[44:42] And right there, actually there's a little nuance that I have so far glossed over. Even if the paths don't intersect with each other, you're still safe to add on one to the total tile count, because if they don't intersect in an X-ed out square, it would mean that they intersect in a tile. And in that special case, that particular tile in the middle would not be touching any of the highlighted edges. So, you're safe to add the one to your count.
[45:04] The point is, this expression right here, really does give you a lower bound for the number of tiles. This in turn was enough to prove the actual bound we want, that expression K squared plus 2K minus 3 that came from the optimal grid tiling, just as long as this part here, the sum of the lengths of those two paths, really is greater than or equal to 2 times K. And this is what we just proved in the last section, using a combination of the arithmetic mean geometric mean inequality with the Erdos-Szekeres theorem.
[45:34] Taking this expression and plugging in K equals 45, you get the numerical answer to the original question. But again, that numerical answer is just a very small part of the point. The real point is about the construction, and then finding some kind of rigorous proof that it is optimal. And it might have taken a while. It might have even taken a fair bit of patience, but we've done exactly that.
[45:59] So, what's the point? What do we learn by seeing how to solve a problem like this? And actually, I think it might be nicer to do this outro face-to-face. You know, I introduced this whole problem as the last IMO problem AI could not solve. This might mean a natural way we could conclude would be to frame it as something like that game four between Lee Sedol and AlphaGo, you know, humanity's last stand before the machines just got categorically better.
[46:23] I imagine another thing a lot of you have probably been thinking is, what is it about this problem that made it so hard for the AIs to solve? There's some natural speculation there, you know, we spent a lot of time with very visual intuition. I imagine that's harder to train for than purely symbolic reasoning. A more subtle point is the one that Thang Luong made, where this is the kind of problem you can't just immediately start writing a solution for. You have to understand it and get a feel for it before you write that solution. That kind of structure is intrinsically harder for a reinforcement learning environment.
[46:54] But if I think about my own personal relationship with this problem, there's a completely different and arguably much more important way that it relates to the broader story unfolding about AI and math right now, that has nothing to do with when AI could and could not solve problems like this.
[47:08] I wrote this video in collaboration with Nishad Deulkar. And when both of us set out to do it, it's not like the goal was to find a new proof to an unsolved problem. The proof obviously already existed. The proof also existed on YouTube. For instance, there's a channel called Dedekind Cuts that covers a lot of IMO problems, including this one.
[47:26] So why make this video? What do we think is the new thing to contribute? To me, knowing a proof is actually only one very small part of what it feels like to deeply understand a given piece of math. This proof in particular was one where Nishad and I looked at it and said, "Okay, I see that this works, but how on earth would you come up with that?"
[47:44] You know, you define this longest increasing subsequence, longest decreasing subsequence, certain association between edges and tiles. But without any leading in context, you can follow the steps of that and be left feeling like it is a complete bolt from out of the blue.
[47:57] In the video itself, I talked about how there's this qualitative difference between finding the construction and then what it feels like to articulate a proof. What I didn't mention is that there is yet another level of engagement that also feels qualitatively different, which is to create a narrative by which a viewer can feel like that proof is almost obvious. And we know the proof is not obvious. Only six of the students solved this. It is a demonstrably hard question. But if we've done our job right, my hope is that by the time we were landing on the proof articulation itself, it didn't feel like that bolt from out of the blue.
[48:30] Now, finding that kind of narrative to me is deeply rewarding, it's very creative. I always feel like I come out understanding a piece of math much better than I did simply by understanding the proof. I think it even helps to give a name to what this other thing is that's not just a proof. And for lack of a better one, I'm just going to call it a motivated explanation.
[48:47] So, stepping outside of this toy problem, to the broader world of what's happening in math right now, where machines are capable of producing proofs to very famous unsolved problems, what you see is a lot of mathematicians stepping back and reflecting on how the purpose of doing mathematics, the practice as they understand it, has always been about furthering human understanding.
[49:07] And the role of proofs, and open problems, has always been one of a guiding light to help people know where and how to push forward that understanding. It's not so much that the solution to the problem is ever going to be something that you plug into an application in the world and get utility out of. It's a lot more subtle than that. It's more like, in order for a human to find these proofs, they have to figure out the patterns of thinking and constructs and new mathematical objects that elevates their understanding enough to make that proof available.
[49:37] But what's useful is not the proof, or even the result, it's all of that surrounding understanding and the spillover effects that it can have into the engineering world.
[49:45] So if you're able to generate proofs that don't necessarily come with human understanding, that kind of completely defeats the point. But this raises a very serious question about how we measure academic progress, because the idea of using proof as a proxy is so deeply ingrained into what we give academic credit for, that it exposes a very stark need for a new, distinct way to measure whether someone's published output really does push forward human understanding.
[50:12] For my part, I actually think this idea of a motivated explanation could do a lot to fill that void. I think that we as a community should try to formalize what we mean by a motivated explanation, and then we should elevate it to have the same status and give the same kind of academic credit that proof historically has. I have many more thoughts on this topic. I wrote a guest post for Terry Tao's blog about this, that I also recorded as a video on this channel. So take a look if you're interested.
[50:39] I am guessing this will be the first of many thoughts I want to express about the whole AI and math matter. For today though, focusing back on this very fun IMO problem from 2025, I want to close with a very nice sentiment from the comments on Patreon. So many of you know, I always post videos early for supporters, and in this case, one of them left a quote from a friend of theirs who had solved this problem.
[51:01] "This question doesn't contribute to a deep understanding of mathematics, nor is it particularly difficult (when compared with mathematical research). Rather, the value of this question lies in the fact that it warmed my heart when I solved it, and it still warms my heart more than a year later. Like a good book or a touching song, the value here is human."
[51:20] "Call me humanist, but I truly believe that the value of this question, as a mathematical discovery, exceeds that of the average PhD thesis."

20 Sep 2026

# ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector

OpenAI's ad collector at `bzr.openai.com` sets a cookie called `__obi`, scoped to `.openai.com`. The value is while you are on ChatGPT and tied to your ChatGPT account. `__obi` is then sent to OpenAI from ordinary websites you visit.

Any company that buys ads on ChatGPT installs a [small piece of OpenAI code](https://developers.openai.com/ads/measurement-pixel?ref=buchodi.com) on its own site, the same way retailers already install Meta and Google tracking code. Loading that code, sends `__obi` to OpenAI along with data about the page you are browsing. This includes products you are searching for, articles you are reading, and purchase behaviors.

The bottom line is that OpenAI can connect what you do on those sites to your ChatGPT account.

I reproduced the full mechanism on my own phone, verified with two independent capture methods, and cross-checked against several months of observed traffic covering 936 distinct advertiser pixels across 1,029 hostnames.

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/b8/53/b853e3d4-3186-409d-9c7f-7da931a60431/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-20-at-5.00.35---PM.png)

## How it works

**Step 1. ChatGPT creates an identifier and signs it.**

On `chatgpt.com`, the client generates 16 random bytes and calls `POST /backend-api/bazaar/obi/sync-token` (or `/backend-anon/` when signed out). The backend returns an RS256 JWT:

```
{
  "iss": "chatgpt-wadi",
  "aud": "bzr.openai.com",
  "purpose": "obi_sync",
  "operation": "set",
  "consent_decision": "analytics_allowed",
  "consent_policy_version": "user_granular_consent_v1",
  "sub": "«redacted: 64-hex account subject»",
  "subject_type": "account_user",
  "obi": "«redacted: 22-char identifier»",
  "exp": "«iat + 60s»"
}
```

`sub` is the account. `obi` is the identifier. The token binds them, is scoped to the collector, and expires in 60 seconds. `bzr` stands for `bazaar`, OpenAI's internal name for the ads platform; `wadi` is the issuing service.

**Step 2. The identifier becomes a cookie on OpenAI's domain.**

The client POSTs `{"token": "«JWT»"}` cross-site to `bzr.openai.com/v1/obi/sync`. The response:

```
Set-Cookie: __obi=«redacted»; Domain=.openai.com; HttpOnly;
            Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; SameSite=none; Secure
```

`SameSite=none` with `Secure` is the configuration a cookie needs to be sent on cross-site requests. `Max-Age` is one year. The `obi` value in the JWT and the value in the cookie are identical.

**Step 3. Advertiser sites send it back.**

Three request classes go from an advertiser's page to OpenAI's hosts. On a phone with `__obi` in the jar, all three carried it:

| Request | Carried `__obi` | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET bzrcdn.openai.com/sdk/oaiq.min.js` | yes | the script load itself |
| `POST bzr.openai.com/v1/sdk/events` with `obref` | yes | conversion events |
| `POST bzr.openai.com/v1/sdk/events`, bare body | yes | the SDK's "no credentials" path |
| `GET bzrcdn.openai.com/pixel-config/…` | no cookie header at all | control |

The first row is particularly interesting. The pixel SDK has a code path that omits credentials, and it does not help: the browser attaches cookies to the `<script src>` request that loads the SDK before any of OpenAI's code runs. By the virtue of loading the tag the identifier is disclosed.

## What travels with it

The same SDK also collects identity from the advertiser's page. The payload separates four sources, labelled by OpenAI itself: `in` for values the advertiser passes deliberately, and `fm`, `ht`, `js` for values the SDK scrapes from form fields, rendered page text, and the tag-manager bus. In observed traffic, scraped identity outnumbered advertiser-supplied identity 685 events to 255.

The tag-manager bus is the largest source of email. The SDK replaces `window.dataLayer.push` with its own function, also reads `adobeDataLayer`, and locates renamed GTM layers by parsing the `l=` parameter off the `gtm.js` script tag. Current versions take email and phone from it. Version 0.1.31 also took names and geography before the scope was narrowed on 27 August.

Email, phone, first and last name are SHA-256 hashed before transmission. Country, region, city and postal code are sent in the clear. Postal code was the most-harvested form field, 100 events across 28 sites.

URLs are reduced to origin plus path before sending; none of 23,929 observed carried a query string. Paths survive, and paths reaching the collector included a medical condition, a debt-solutions funnel and a litigation intake form.

Automatic matching was enabled for 638 of 881 pixels with a known setting, including every credit and lending advertiser observed. It is controlled from OpenAI's Ads Manager. A denylist excludes passwords, one-time codes, card numbers, SSN, date of birth, medical history, diagnosis and court fields.
